1) Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infection (eg, Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus) — Most likely. Timing (lesions starting ~2 weeks after invasive cosmetic procedures), lack of response to topical antibacterials/steroids, and common association of non-tuberculous mycobacteria with post-procedural skin/soft-tissue infections make this the top concern.

2) Granulomatous foreign-body / fat-graft reaction (fat necrosis or foreign-body granuloma) — Next most likely. Autologous fat transfer can provoke localized inflammatory nodules or granulomas weeks after grafting; these may appear as firm papules/nodules and do not respond to topical antibiotics/steroids.

3) Cutaneous HPV infection (verruca) inoculated at procedure sites — Possible. Verrucous “wart-like” appearance fits, though HPV incubation is often longer; procedural trauma can unmask or spread lesions.

4) Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus) — Less likely but possible given the post-procedural timing (incubation 2–8 weeks) and facial location; classically produces umbilicated papules rather than verrucous lesions.

5) Deep fungal or atypical bacterial (common bacterial) infection or hypertrophic scarring/keloid — Less likely given failure of topical mupirocin and corticosteroid; included as lower-probability alternatives.

Recommended immediate next diagnostic steps (highest yield)
- Punch biopsy of an active lesion for histopathology (H&E) with special stains (AFB/Ziehl-Neelsen for mycobacteria, Fite if available, and fungal stains such as PAS/GMS). 
- Send fresh tissue for aerobic bacterial culture, mycobacterial culture (specifically request rapid growers like M. chelonae/abscessus), and fungal culture.
- Consider PCR on lesion tissue for poxvirus (molluscum) and HPV if histology is inconclusive.

Additional recommended tests to assess host risk
- HIV test and fasting glucose or HbA1c (to screen for immunosuppression/diabetes).
- Photograph lesions for documentation and clinical follow-up.

Immediate management advice pending results
- Avoid further topical steroid use or empiric systemic antibiotics without culture guidance.
- If mycobacterial infection is later confirmed, targeted systemic antimicrobials (eg, macrolide +/- others guided by susceptibility) and surgical debridement/ excision are often required.
- If granulomatous reaction is favored by biopsy, options include intralesional steroids, surgical removal of discrete nodules, or systemic therapy guided by dermatology/plastics.
